title: Mildred the perfectionist
summary: Norvo explains Mildred's demand for correctness in music and in life, and says he respects such perfectionists.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Yeah, that's right. Well, the thing was I mean -- I -- you know -- you had -- I know I did -- the greatest sympathy anyway for how she felt because the way I read it was, she couldn't stand any hypocrisy of any kind --
-- and she didn't like any dumbness of any kind, you know, she looked for talent and, as you said, she had this tremendous intuitive perception about people and what she heard --
-- musically, bad music infuriated her. Which it does -- can very well do anybody who cares. Wouldn't you say so?
Bad music. Bad music made her furious.

And so I think, you know, I mean -- she would get into one of those, you know, things of being -- having -- be in a rage about something and say things about some body or some thing, it was understandable because --
Well, let's face one thing, with people
that are like Mildred, they're perfectionists, they like --
They don't back down for any quarter from quarry from themselves --
-- yeah, but they -- they make a point of knowing what is right. She knows the way things should be cooked. She knows the way they should be served, she knows about a lot of things --
-- and she knows what is correct.
I can't argue with that in anybody. Whether it's an artist or whether it's any line of work --
-- anybody that wants to be that way. I respect them for it --
I think some are more tolerant talent than others.
